2026-09-25

Session 5 :: PCA & Hierarchical Clustering

Learning objectives

By the end of this session you should be able to:

  • Explain why PCA looks for directions of largest variance, and when it helps to scale. the input first.
  • Run PCA with prcomp() and read the parts of the result you actually use: sdev, rotation, x.
  • Produce a scree plot and a biplot, in base R and in ggplot2, and say what each one shows.
  • Use the common rules of thumb for how many PCs to keep, and their limits.
  • Compute distances with dist(), build a tree with hclust(), and cut it into groups with cutree().
  • Put the two together on a small transcriptomics-style matrix.

Two datasets today. Teaching uses the built-in iris (150 × 4). The practice at the end uses a toy expression matrix (200 genes × 18 samples, 3 groups), shipped as data/expr_toy.rds.

Part I — Principal Component Analysis

PCA

Why PCA?

Real datasets often have many correlated variables. Looking at them two at a time does not scale — 4 features give 6 scatter plots, 20 features give 190.

When two variables are strongly correlated, one direction already carries most of what both of them say. PCA finds such directions, ranks them by how much variance they capture, and lets you plot the first couple on one page.

Three places this comes up in bioinformatics:

  • Sample QC — spot an outlier sample on PC1–PC2 before any differential analysis.
  • Batch effects — check whether the largest source of variance is your biology or the day the samples were run.
  • Compression — pass a few PCs into a downstream model instead of thousands of genes.

The pairs-plot frustration is the motivation. PCA is “give me the two most informative plots instead of 190”.

What PCA does

  • PC1 — the direction of largest variance in the data.
  • PC2 — the direction of largest variance at right angles to PC1.
  • PC\(k\) — largest variance orthogonal to all earlier PCs.
  • There are at most \(\min(n-1,\ p)\) PCs.

The transformation is a rotation of the coordinate axes. Nothing is lost until you decide to drop some components — that is the step that actually reduces dimensionality.

Stress “rotation first, reduction later”. The reduction is a choice you make, not something prcomp does for you.

Step 1 — center, and usually scale

iris_num <- iris[, 1:4]
apply(iris_num, 2, var)                 # variances differ across columns
Sepal.Length  Sepal.Width Petal.Length  Petal.Width 
   0.6856935    0.1899794    3.1162779    0.5810063 
iris_z <- scale(iris_num)               # center + divide by SD
round(apply(iris_z, 2, mean), 10)       # ~0
Sepal.Length  Sepal.Width Petal.Length  Petal.Width 
           0            0            0            0 
round(apply(iris_z, 2, sd),   10)       # 1
Sepal.Length  Sepal.Width Petal.Length  Petal.Width 
           1            1            1            1
  • Centering subtracts the column mean; it does not change variances.
  • Scaling divides by the SD, so every column has SD 1. PCA then runs on the correlation matrix rather than the covariance matrix.

A rule of thumb: variables in the same units and comparable spread can be left unscaled; variables on different units are usually better scaled, so one large-range column does not dominate PC1 on its own.

Centering alone leaves Petal.Length (largest variance) dominating PC1. Scaling equalises the columns and can rotate the PCs noticeably.

Step 2 — prcomp()

pca <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
names(pca)
[1] "sdev"     "rotation" "center"   "scale"    "x"

The parts you use most:

  • pca$sdev — standard deviation of each PC (\(\sqrt{\text{eigenvalue}}\)).
  • pca$rotation — the loadings: how variables combine into PCs (one row per variable).
  • pca$x — the scores: where each observation lands (one row per observation).

The common mix-up: rotation is about variables (rows = genes/features), x is about observations (rows = samples). “Rotation is variables, x is samples.”

The summary() table

pca <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)
Importance of components:
                          PC1    PC2     PC3     PC4
Standard deviation     1.7084 0.9560 0.38309 0.14393
Proportion of Variance 0.7296 0.2285 0.03669 0.00518
Cumulative Proportion  0.7296 0.9581 0.99482 1.00000

Read the Proportion of Variance row first — it is the headline. For standardised iris, PC1 ≈ 73 % and PC2 ≈ 23 %, so the first two axes together carry about 96 %.

This is the number to quote when someone asks how much of the data a 2-D PCA plot actually shows.

Variance explained — scree plot

Base R — screeplot()

pca <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)
screeplot(pca, type = "lines",
          main = "")
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "#D55E00")

ggplot2 — a bit more control

df <- data.frame(
  PC  = factor(paste0("PC", 1:4),
               levels = paste0("PC", 1:4)),
  eig = pca$sdev^2)

ggplot(df, aes(PC, eig, group = 1)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = 2,
             colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(y = "Eigenvalue")

The dashed line marks eigenvalue = 1 (the Kaiser rule). Two PCs sit above it for standardised iris.

The eigenvalue-1 line only means something after scaling, because scaling makes the average eigenvalue exactly 1.

Loadings — what each PC means

pca <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)
round(pca$rotation, 2)
               PC1   PC2   PC3   PC4
Sepal.Length  0.52 -0.38  0.72  0.26
Sepal.Width  -0.27 -0.92 -0.24 -0.12
Petal.Length  0.58 -0.02 -0.14 -0.80
Petal.Width   0.56 -0.07 -0.63  0.52
  • Rows are the original variables, columns are the PCs.
  • A large absolute value means the variable contributes strongly to that PC.
  • The sign gives the direction of the contribution.

For standardised iris, PC1 is positive on all four measurements — an overall “flower size” axis. PC2 puts Sepal.Width opposite the petal measurements — a shape contrast.

Loadings answer “what does this axis mean” — usually the question a collaborator actually cares about.

The biplot

Base R — biplot()

pca <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)
biplot(pca, cex = 0.6,
       col = c("grey60", "#D55E00"))

ggplot2 — coloured by species

sc <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
sc$Species <- iris$Species
L <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation) * 2.5
L$var <- rownames(L)

ggplot(sc, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = Species), alpha = .8) +
  geom_segment(data = L,
    aes(0, 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
    arrow = arrow(length = unit(.15, "cm")),
    colour = "#D55E00") +
  geom_text(data = L,
    aes(PC1 * 1.1, PC2 * 1.1, label = var),
    colour = "#D55E00", size = 3)

Points are the scores; arrows are the loadings. Arrows close together suggest correlated variables; an arrow’s length reflects how well that variable is shown in these two PCs.

Common misreading: a point’s position relative to an arrow tip. Only the arrow’s direction and length carry meaning.

How many PCs to keep?

Three common rules, none of them definitive:

  1. Kaiser — keep PCs with eigenvalue > 1 (meaningful only after scaling).
  2. Cumulative variance — keep enough PCs to reach, say, 80–90 %.
  3. Scree elbow — the visual bend in the plot.

These are guides, not rules. When it matters, a downstream measure — for example classification accuracy as a function of \(k\) — is more reliable than any single heuristic.

Many papers report 2 PCs because that is what fits on a slide. Worth naming as a mild, real bias in how PCA gets used.

PCA — things to watch for

What you see A likely reason
One variable seems to be PC1 Unscaled data with mismatched units — try scale. = TRUE
PCs look like the raw features Variables barely correlated — little to reduce
A big PC that tracks batch A confounder worth addressing, not ignoring
First two PCs explain very little The signal is genuinely high-dimensional

“Forgot to scale” is behind most “my PCA looks odd” questions.

Part II — Hierarchical Clustering

Hierarchical Clustering

Clustering — the goal

Unsupervised: no labels, just the question are there natural groups here?

Two families to know:

  • Partitioning (k-means, PAM) — you choose \(k\) first; you get \(k\) flat groups.
  • Hierarchical — build a tree of nested groupings, then cut it wherever you like to get any \(k\).

Agglomerative hierarchical clustering works like this:

  1. every observation starts as its own cluster,
  2. repeatedly merge the two closest clusters,
  3. stop when a single cluster remains,
  4. cut the tree at a chosen height to read off groups.

The tree is built once; “choosing k” is just deciding where to cut it — a different workflow from k-means.

Distance — the input to hclust()

iris_z <- scale(iris[, 1:4])
d      <- dist(iris_z, method = "euclidean")

as.matrix(d)[1:5, 1:5] |> round(2)      # first 5 x 5 block
     1    2    3    4    5
1 0.00 1.17 0.84 1.10 0.26
2 1.17 0.00 0.52 0.43 1.38
3 0.84 0.52 0.00 0.28 0.99
4 1.10 0.43 0.28 0.00 1.25
5 0.26 1.38 0.99 1.25 0.00

The same scaling point returns here: with very different units, dist() is dominated by whichever variable has the largest range, so it is usually worth scaling first.

cor(as.vector(dist(iris[, 1:4])),
    as.vector(dist(scale(iris[, 1:4]))))
[1] 0.9529472

Deliberately the same lesson as PCA, twice: unscaled distance follows the largest-numbered column, not the most interesting one.

Linkage — distance between clusters

Once points form clusters, you need a rule for the distance between two clusters. Four common choices behave differently:

d <- dist(scale(iris[, 1:4]))
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2,3,2,1))
plot(hclust(d, method = "single"),
     labels = FALSE, main = "single",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
plot(hclust(d, method = "complete"),
     labels = FALSE, main = "complete",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
par(op)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2,3,2,1))
plot(hclust(d, method = "average"),
     labels = FALSE, main = "average",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
plot(hclust(d, method = "ward.D2"),
     labels = FALSE, main = "ward.D2",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
par(op)
  • single — minimum pairwise distance; can produce long, chained clusters.
  • complete — maximum pairwise distance; compact clusters.
  • average — the mean; a middle ground.
  • ward.D2 — minimises the increase in within-cluster variance; a common default for continuous data.

A comb-shaped dendrogram (one big cluster, many singletons) usually points to single linkage — the first thing to switch away from.

Cutting the tree

hclust() returns a tree; cutree() turns it into flat labels.

iris_z <- scale(iris[, 1:4])
hc <- hclust(dist(iris_z), method = "ward.D2")
cl <- cutree(hc, k = 3)

table(cluster = cl, species = iris$Species)
       species
cluster setosa versicolor virginica
      1     49          0         0
      2      1         27         2
      3      0         23        48

table(cluster, truth) is a quick check when the truth is known. For iris with Ward linkage, setosa comes out cleanly; versicolor and virginica overlap in feature space and mix a little.

Cluster numbers are arbitrary labels — nothing is implied by “cluster 1 vs 3”.

Checking your clusters

Cutting a dendrogram always returns groups — whether or not real structure exists. Two quick numeric sanity checks:

library(cluster)
d  <- dist(scale(iris[, 1:4]))
hc <- hclust(d, method = "ward.D2")
cl <- cutree(hc, k = 3)

mean(silhouette(cl, d)[, "sil_width"])   # -1 to 1, higher = more separated
[1] 0.446689
cor(d, cophenetic(hc))                    # 0 to 1, tree vs. original distances
[1] 0.8226304
  • Silhouette width compares each point’s distance to its own cluster against the next-nearest one. Here it comes out middling (~0.45) — matching the versicolor/virginica overlap seen in table(cluster, species).
  • Cophenetic correlation checks how faithfully the tree’s merge heights reproduce the original distances (~0.82 here — a reasonably good summary).

Both are diagnostics, not proof: pair them with table(cluster, truth) when a known grouping exists, and treat any fixed cutoff as a rough guide, not a law.

See ?cluster::silhouette and ?cophenetic. Avoid stating a single hard threshold as universal — it depends on the data and the distance/linkage combination used.

Colouring the dendrogram

hc <- hclust(dist(scale(iris[, 1:4])), method = "ward.D2")
plot(hc, labels = FALSE, main = "iris — ward.D2",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc, k = 3,
            border = c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "#009E73"))

rect.hclust() draws the boxes for a chosen \(k\). This three-colour set (orange / blue / green) stays distinguishable under the common forms of colour-blindness.

Heatmap: matrix and dendrogram together

heatmap() clusters rows (and, by default, columns) and draws the data matrix next to the dendrogram — a fast way to show sample/feature structure at a glance, and the natural next step from a plain dendrogram.

iris_z  <- scale(iris[, 1:4])
sp_col  <- c(setosa = "#D55E00", versicolor = "#0072B2", virginica = "#009E73")

heatmap(iris_z,
        hclustfun = function(d) hclust(d, method = "ward.D2"),
        Colv = NA, labRow = NA, margins = c(6, 2),
        RowSideColors = sp_col[iris$Species])

The side colour bar (orange / blue / green, same palette as rect.hclust() above) shows the true species next to the tree heatmap() built on its own — a quick visual check of where the clustering agrees or disagrees with a known label.

Colv = NA skips clustering the 4 columns here, since with only 4 variables that dendrogram adds little. Packages such as pheatmap or ComplexHeatmap give more layout control (multiple annotation rows, custom colour scales) at the cost of an extra dependency — heatmap() is worth knowing first because it ships with base R.

PCA + clustering together

The two techniques answer complementary questions — PCA asks which axes carry the variance, clustering asks which observations group together. A natural combination: cluster the data, then show the clusters on PC1–PC2.

iris_z <- scale(iris[, 1:4])
pca <- prcomp(iris_z)
hc  <- hclust(dist(iris_z), method = "ward.D2")
cl  <- factor(cutree(hc, k = 3))

df <- data.frame(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2],
                 cluster = cl, species = iris$Species)

ggplot(df, aes(PC1, PC2)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = cluster, shape = species), size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(colour = cluster), level = 0.68) +
  labs(subtitle = "colour = cluster, shape = true species")

This is the figure most collaborators want: do my clusters agree with my known groups? It is also the shape of Task 4 in the practice.

Summary

Three things to take away

  1. When variables live on different units, scaling before PCA or clustering usually matters more than any other choice you make here.
  2. Read the summary(pca) proportion-of-variance row before anything else.
  3. In hierarchical clustering, linkage often matters more than the distance metric; ward.D2 is a reasonable default, and single is prone to chaining.

A few more, briefly:

  • prcomp() gives you sdev, rotation, and x — most work uses those three.
  • Kaiser, cumulative variance, and the scree elbow are guides, not laws.
  • hclust() + cutree() + table(cluster, truth) is a fast sanity loop on any small dataset.
